title: Fast Fallback Paths: latency vs cost snapshot (draft)
content:
Purpose:
A short working snapshot comparing three fast-fallback strategies for maintaining SLOs under transient capacity pressure. This is a lightweight bench used by product/console and runtime to decide which fallback(s) to prototype for Q2 rollout. Not exhaustive — this is exploratory notes + raw numbers for discussion.

High-level summary:
- We measured p50/p90/p99 latency and approximate $/1k queries for three strategies, on the same baseline model (redwood-llama-13b-quant) and identical workload generator: 60% short queries (<=40 tokens), 30% medium (40-200), 10% long (200-1024).
- Strategies: (A) model-variant fallback (lighter model when queue crosses threshold), (B) early-exit heuristic (stop deeper layers for short queries via shallow-decode policy), (C) KV-prefetch+slot-tiling (speculative KV+compact tiling to preserve full model but amortize token work).
- On short transients (1–15s spike) model-variant gives the cleanest p99 improvement vs cost, early-exit yields best p50 uplift with modest cost reduction, prefetched tiling keeps quality but is the most expensive operationally to implement.

Experiment configuration:
- Hardware: 4xA100-80GB pool (single region), all requests routed to single logical cluster.
- Baseline runtime config: batching window = 20ms, dynamic batching enabled, kv-cache enabled.
- Load generator: Poisson arrivals scaled to create sustained concurrency of 120 tokens/sec baseline and transient 10x bursts lasting 5–12s.
- Measurement window: 30 trial runs each strategy, collect p50/p90/p99 of server-side latency (ms), token-cost estimate (GPU-seconds converted to $ using $0.40/gpu-minute), and a small qualitative quality note (0–1 drop observed by automated eval).

Raw aggregated numbers (median across trials):

Strategy | p50 (ms) | p90 (ms) | p99 (ms) | est $ / 1k queries | quality delta
---------|----------|----------|----------|-------------------|-----------
Baseline | 110      | 270      | 900      | $3.80             | 0.0
Model-Variant (A) | 125      | 320      | 420      | $2.10             | -0.06
Early-Exit (B)    | 85       | 200      | 650      | $2.75             | -0.10
KV-prefetch+Tiling (C) | 105      | 240      | 480      | $3.20             | -0.02

Notes on table:
- Cost: dollar-per-1k computed from measured GPU-seconds for each run; numbers rounded. Baseline cost is higher because p99 tails cause longer GPU occupation per query.
- Quality delta: rough delta in BLEU/ROUGE-style proxy used for quick automated check (negative means slight degradation). These are coarse; real human eval pending.

ASCII visual sketch (p99 bar normalized):
Baseline  : |||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||| (900ms)
A (variant): ||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||| (420ms)
B (early)  : |||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||| (650ms)
C (kv)     : ||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||| (480ms)

Observations:
- Model-Variant (A): biggest p99 win (reduction ~53% vs baseline) and biggest cost win (~45% cheaper). Quality hit small but visible (-0.06). This is attractive when client can tolerate slightly lower fidelity on tail calls. Implementation complexity: low (route to smaller model + model catalog management + routing policy).
- Early-Exit (B): improves median significantly and modest p90, but p99 still elevated vs A. Quality impact somewhat larger; early-exit heuristics are brittle for medium-length prompts because layer-skipping can truncate reasoning. Implementation complexity: medium (requires model support for conditional layer exit and per-request hinting).
- KV-prefetch+Tiling (C): keeps quality close to baseline (best fidelity), moderate p99 improvement and moderate cost reduction. Operational complexity high (tiling/prefetch plumbing, eviction semantics) but aligns with longer-term amortization goals.

Edge cases / caveats:
- Bursts longer than 15s flip the economics: model-variant degrades perceived quality across sustained session flows and can increase user retries.
- Our simple quality proxy underweights subtle hallucinations; early-exit may have more severe failure modes on some instruction tasks. Need targeted eval sets per client vertical.
- Cost model excludes infra network egress and storage IO for prefetching; include those in formal TCO.

Recommended next steps (short run):
1) Prototype A (model-variant routing) as a canary on a low-traffic tenant and add per-route toggle in console. Goal: validate human-facing quality delta over 2 weeks. Owner: Ravi.
2) Build a controlled early-exit sandbox and run focused eval on instruction-following prompts to characterize catastrophic failure modes. Owner: Sofia.
3) De-risk KV-prefetch work by extracting a minimal tiling shim that can be toggled per-model; collect operational telemetry for complexity estimate. Owner: Liam.

Rollout checklist for A (model-variant):
- [ ] Add new model catalog entry (redwood-llama-13b-lite) + perf profile
- [ ] Add routing policy: p99-lag threshold = 600ms -> route 30% traffic to variant; incremental step-down policy
- [ ] Add telemetry: per-route fidelity metric, user-initiated-correction rate, and session continuity metric
- [ ] QA: manual review on 200 golden prompts across verticals
- [ ] Canary: 2% traffic for 72h -> examine metrics -> 10% -> 30%

Measurement notes for engineering:
- Keep trace IDs stable across strategies to enable trace-level diffing.
- Record GPU occupancy per-step to separate batching vs exec savings.
- Export raw token-level timings for later percentile analysis (we used aggregated server-side latency which hides queue-time contribution).

Open questions:
- What is the acceptable quality delta per SLA segment? (PLG free tier tolerances likely different from enterprise).
- Do we prefer a single fallback strategy globally or allow model-by-model policy? (product/console tradeoff).
- Can we combine A+B (route to variant + early-exit on variant) and get multiplicative wins? Quick experiments suggest diminishing returns and compounded quality risk.

Appendix: quick trial traces (one-picked example, timings in ms)
- Baseline trace: queue 120 -> batch 42 -> exec 620 -> total 820
- A (variant) trace: queue 80 -> batch 28 -> exec 160 -> total 268
- B (early-exit) trace: queue 40 -> batch 12 -> exec 450 -> total 502
- C (kv-tiling) trace: queue 60 -> batch 20 -> exec 220 -> total 300

Concluding note:
This doc is a conversation starter. My leaning: kick off model-variant prototype (A) quickly because it gives the largest p99 and cost wins with the lowest engineering ramp. Parallelize a narrow early-exit evaluation for short-instruction tasks. Keep KV-prefetch on the roadmap for workloads where fidelity is paramount.

Questions / feedback welcome — add notes inline or ping #serving-runtime.

-- Ava
